analysis.one_liner: Bars medical debt from credit reports and bans lenders from using it in credit decisions.
analysis.headline: Backed by 60 House Democrats, the bill died in the Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have kept medical bills off credit reports and required the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to bar lenders from using medical debt when deciding whether to approve a loan or credit card. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans with medical debt on their credit reports would see it removed, which typically raises credit scores and makes it easier to rent an apartment, buy a car, get a mortgage, or sometimes pass an employment check. Because medical bills often land on credit reports even when people are paying them or disputing them, the bill would also protect people who got sick, not people who were financially irresponsible. A second provision would stop lenders from refusing credit or pricing it higher based on medical debt information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills on credit reports

how_it_helps.text: Adds medical debt to the list of information consumer reporting agencies are prohibited from including on a credit report, covering even debts placed with collection agencies or written off.
Defines medical debt broadly as any debt tied to receiving medical services, products, or devices, so the exclusion covers hospital bills, doctor bills, and related collections.
Requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, within one year of enactment, to change its rules so creditors cannot obtain or use medical debt information when deciding whether to extend credit.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and specialty medical-debt reporting agencies would lose a stream of data they sell to lenders, and collection agencies would lose one of their main leverage points for pressuring people to pay. Lenders would lose medical debt as an underwriting signal, and they argue that could mean slightly higher prices or tighter credit spread across all borrowers. People who owed the underlying medical bills would still owe them; the bill changes reporting and lending decisions, not the debt itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders

drawbacks.text: The bill does not reduce or forgive any medical debt; collectors could still call, sue, garnish, and pursue payment — it would only stop the debt from appearing on credit reports or being used in lending decisions.

Lenders argue medical debt is predictive of whether someone repays loans, so removing it from underwriting could lead them to raise prices or tighten credit for everyone to cover the added uncertainty — a cost that would fall partly on borrowers who never had medical debt.
A one-size federal exclusion also sweeps in debts regardless of how legitimate they are, going further than the narrower wait-time rules the credit bureaus had already adopted voluntarily.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: medical debt is the most common collection item on credit reports, and it often reflects bad luck with health insurance rather than unwillingness to pay, so its removal would meaningfully improve access to housing and credit for millions. The honest costs are that the underlying debt still exists, and lenders lose one predictive signal, which they claim — without strong evidence in this record — could nudge credit costs up for everyone. On balance the bill's benefits concentrate on people already hurt by illness, while the costs are diffuse and mostly fall on data brokers and lenders.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, the chair never brought it up for a hearing or vote, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Katie Porter introduced the bill on October 19, 2023, with 23 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
Six days later it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which holds jurisdiction over credit reporting law.

Support grew to 59 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, but the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and the complete action history shows no activity after the October 2023 referral.
The bill expired on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended, and all pending bills die at that point without any action needed from opponents.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, medical-debt collection firms, and lenders that use medical debt in underwriting keep the status quo — the debt stays on credit reports and remains usable in lending decisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders

for.name: Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 23 original cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 59 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, growing the list to 59, though all support came from one party.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral; the record shows no committee action at all.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, so it lacked the bipartisan support that typically moves a bill through committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 59 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans without a vote.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and specialty medical bureaus)
industries.note: They sell credit files, and medical debt is one of the most common collection items on them; the bill would strip that data out nationwide. Their business interest runs against the millions of consumers whose scores are dragged down by illness-related bills.
A bill showing up on a credit report is a collector's main lever for getting people to pay quickly. Removing that lever would weaken their collections while leaving the underlying debt legally owed.

They would lose medical debt as an underwriting input, which they say helps them predict repayment. Some might gain customers whose scores improve, but the industry position was that it prefers to keep using the data.
